summary: The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol measures one-way network characteristics such as delay and loss. Precise one-way measurement became practical with good time sources such as GPS, and OWAMP lets different implementations interoperate. It was later updated by RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545.

plainLanguage.summary: OWAMP defines how hosts can measure network delay and packet loss in one direction. One protocol sets up the test over TCP; another sends timestamped test packets over UDP. RFC 4656 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545.

questions: how to measure one-way packet loss
how does owamp measure one-way delay
subtitle: A standard way for two hosts to measure delay and loss in one direction at a time.

tldr.problem: One-way delay and loss metrics existed, but measurement systems lacked a standard for starting test streams and exchanging packets in an interoperable way.
tldr.mechanism: OWAMP-Control uses TCP to set up, start and stop tests and retrieve results. OWAMP-Test sends scheduled UDP packets containing sequence numbers and timestamps, with optional authentication or encryption.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines interoperable one-way active measurement and allocates TCP port 861 for control. It has been updated by RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545.

today: RFC 4656 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7717, RFC 7718 and RFC 8545.

sections.title: Why Measure One-Way Performance
sections.content:
The IP Performance Metrics working group had defined metrics for one-way packet delay and loss, but systems did not have a shared method to start test streams and exchange measurement packets. More widely available accurate time sources made high-precision one-way measurements practical.

OWAMP defines interoperable active measurements. Its design goals include separating test control from test traffic, supporting small packets, and providing optional authentication and encryption. Encrypted mode is intended to make timestamp changes detectable.
sections.plainLanguage: One-way measurements show how a network behaves in a single direction, but they need accurate clocks and a common test method. OWAMP defines that method and can protect test traffic.

sections.title: Control and Test Roles
sections.content:
OWAMP contains two related protocols. OWAMP-Control arranges, starts and stops test sessions and retrieves results. OWAMP-Test sends the measurement packets between a sender and receiver. Control runs over TCP; test traffic runs over UDP.

The RFC defines five logical roles: Session-Sender, Session-Receiver, Server, Control-Client and Fetch-Client. One host may fill several roles. The control client opens a TCP connection to the server on port 861, and the connection remains open while test sessions run.
sections.plainLanguage: OWAMP uses one connection to arrange and manage a test, and a separate packet stream to perform it. The sender, receiver, server and clients are roles; one host can fill several of them.

sections.title: Choosing a Security Mode
sections.content:
After a TCP connection opens, the server sends a greeting that lists supported modes: unauthenticated (1), authenticated (2) and encrypted (4). The greeting also carries a random Challenge, a Salt and a Count used to derive a key from a shared passphrase. Count must be a power of 2 and at least 1024.

The client selects a supported mode in Set-Up-Response. For protected modes, it identifies a shared secret with KeyID and sends a token containing a challenge and session keys encrypted with AES in CBC mode. The server responds with Server-Start; an Accept value of zero means it will continue. In authenticated and encrypted modes, OWAMP-Control encrypts later messages and adds an HMAC-SHA1 value truncated to 128 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The server lists the security modes it supports, and the client chooses one. Protected modes use a shared secret to establish session keys; later control messages are encrypted and checked with an HMAC.

sections.title: Creating, Running and Retrieving Sessions
sections.content:
The client sends Request-Session messages describing the sender and receiver, packet count, schedule, start time, packet padding, timeout and packet type. The server responds to each request with Accept-Session and may reject it. A packet not received within the session's Timeout after it was sent is counted as lost.

After accepted requests, Start-Sessions begins the tests. While tests run, Stop-Sessions is the only available command, and either the client or server may send it. The message reports each session's next sequence number and ranges of packets that the sender skipped. Fetch-Session identifies a session and requested sequence range; the returned packet records include send and receive timing information and the TTL or Hop Limit.
sections.plainLanguage: The client describes the test and the server accepts or rejects it. The client starts the accepted tests, either side can stop them, and a fetch request retrieves the recorded results.

sections.title: Reproducible Packet Schedules
sections.content:
The sender and receiver need the same schedule so the receiver can determine when a missing packet should have been sent. A schedule repeats a list of slots. A slot either waits an exponentially distributed random interval with a specified mean or waits a fixed interval.

One random slot describes a Poisson stream; one fixed slot describes a periodic stream. To make random intervals reproducible across implementations, the RFC specifies an algorithm using exact constants and unsigned 64-bit arithmetic. Uniform random values are produced using AES in counter mode with the session identifier as the seed.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver follows the same schedule as the sender, so it can identify when a packet should have arrived. OWAMP defines how both ends produce the same random schedule values.

sections.title: Test Packets and Their Timestamps
sections.content:
Each OWAMP-Test packet is a UDP datagram with a sequence number, a timestamp, a clock-error estimate and optional padding. The sequence number starts at zero. The timestamp uses the NTP format: seconds since 1 January 1900 followed by a fractional part. The receiver timestamps arrival and records the sequence number, send and receive times, and TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit.

The minimum data segment is 14 octets in unauthenticated mode and 48 octets in authenticated or encrypted mode. Authenticated mode encrypts and authenticates the first 16-octet block while leaving the timestamp readable. Encrypted mode protects the first 32 octets, including the timestamp. Packets are protected independently, so a lost, repeated or reordered packet does not prevent processing another packet. The receiver records duplicates; packets with failed authentication or implausible send times must be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: A test packet carries its sequence number and send time, along with an estimate of clock accuracy. The receiver records its arrival time too, which lets the results show delay and loss. Authenticated mode leaves the timestamp readable; encrypted mode protects it.

sections.title: Security and Resource Limits
sections.content:
Authenticated mode is intended to prevent unauthorized use of a server and tampering with results by an attacker who cannot read the test traffic. Encrypted mode aims to make it difficult for a middle party to make results appear better than they are. By default, servers must reject receiver addresses that are neither the control client's address nor an address the server controls. Test packets must not use spoofed source addresses.

Servers must limit network capacity and memory use, with conservative default limits. The RFC requires HMAC verification before data is used. It explains that OWAMP uses its own protection because stream-based TLS does not suit independently lost UDP packets, DTLS anti-replay would interfere with measuring duplicates, and IPsec cannot authenticate only part of a packet as authenticated mode needs. Long-term keys are managed manually.
sections.plainLanguage: OWAMP's security modes help control server access and prevent changes to measurement data. Servers must limit resource use and reject requests that could direct test traffic at an unrelated host.
